rashi:a4.1: Kulfei tavei: great blows, over this teaching. For he would teach me that the appraisal of orphans’ property, according to Rabbi Meir, is sixty days, and I would object to him: But Rabbi Meir said thirty! And he said to me: If he comes to proclaim on consecutive days, it is thirty days, whether for orphans or for consecrated property.
rashi:a4.2: And if he comes to proclaim on Mondays and Thursdays, which are the days of judgment, the appraisal is sixty days, and the days of proclamation are eighteen. Go and count eight weeks from a Monday: that gives you fifty-six days, and they contain sixteen Mondays and Thursdays. Add four more days, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday: that makes sixty days from when the proclamation began, and they contain eighteen days of proclamation.
rashi:a6.1: One does not attend to the property of orphans: to sell it.
rashi:a6.2: Interest consuming it: they owed money at interest to a gentile.
rashi:a6.3: Because of sustenance: for as long as she has not collected her marriage contract she is sustained from their property, and that is a loss to them.
rashi:a8.1: If we say with a gentile creditor: who takes interest, and that is why one attends.
rashi:a8.2: Will he comply: and wait the days of our proclamation without interest?
rashi:a10.1: With one who claims her marriage contract in court: since she then no longer has sustenance, the orphans lose nothing by waiting.
rashi:a11.1: We should not attend to her: to pay her marriage contract, since from now on her sustenance is no longer upon the orphans.
rashi:a11.2: Since we attended to her at the outset: at the start of her claim for her marriage contract, to make her lose her sustenance.
rashi:a11.3: We attend to her in the end: to collect her marriage contract for her.
rashi:a16.1: This is not difficult; it is Rabbi Meir, who says a wife’s marriage contract is from intermediate land: that is, from [the husband] himself, for example if he divorced her; and it teaches us that from orphans it is from inferior land.
rashi:a18.1: As we answered: with a gentile creditor.
rashi:a20.1: When the one obligated admits: their father admitted at the time of his death.
rashi:a20.2: All of them too, when the one obligated admits: and with a Jewish creditor.
rashi:a21.1: A divorcée: she has no sustenance.
rashi:a23.1: That of Rabbi Yoḥanan: who said that a wife’s marriage contract is collected from orphans.
rashi:a23.2: We teach it because of favor: so that the men will find favor in the eyes of the women and they will marry them. Therefore even a divorcée too.
rashi:a24.1: Let them go after those who left them: let them die like their father, who left them this money.
rashi:a25.1: They are not fit to perform a mitzva: since they are minors; rather, let him wait until they grow up.
rashi:a25.2: He placed bundles in his hand: their father gave his creditor coins, or silver and gold, as a pledge at the time of his death, and did not manage to take the document back from him.
rashi:a26.1: Where they excommunicated him: the court [excommunicated] their father because he would not pay this man his debt, and he died in his excommunication. Now there is no need to worry about bundles, for he would have paid him only in court, so that they would lift his ban.
rashi:a27.1: They sent from there: where they excommunicated him and he died in his excommunication. All those mishnayot above that said “one attends” are established [as speaking of this case].
rashi:a27.2: And the halakha follows Rav Huna: that where they did not excommunicate him, one is concerned about bundles.
tosafot:a8.1: We learned: the appraisal of orphans, etc. What are we dealing with? If we say with a gentile creditor, will he comply? And if you will say: why does it need to object to Rav Asi from our mishna? It could have objected from Rav Asi’s own statement, where he said that one does not attend to the property of orphans unless interest is consuming it: what are we dealing with in this “one does not attend”? If we say with a gentile creditor, will he comply and wait until they grow up? And if with a Jewish creditor, do we let him consume interest? One can say: from Rav Asi’s statement it could not object, since it can be established where [the creditor] did not claim from them, and it really speaks of a gentile creditor. That is why one does not attend to the property to pay the debt unless interest is consuming it; [then] one attends even if the gentile did not claim his debt from them, so that the interest will not grow upon them. But from our mishna it objects well, since certainly, from the fact that the court goes down to appraise, it speaks of where he claimed from them. Therefore it objects: if with a gentile creditor, will he comply until after the proclamation is completed, so as not to increase the interest? And if he will not comply, then perhaps they will lose more by the extension of time than they will gain; for certainly, if we do not know whether we gain or not, they would not need a proclamation, as the Talmud says shortly about Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement.
tosafot:a24.1: Rav Naḥman said: At first I would not attend to orphans… from then on I would attend: The halakha follows Rav Naḥman in [matters of] law, that one attends to the property of orphans. And so too it is in the chapter HaKotev (Ketubot 84a), on what we learned: One who died and left a wife, a creditor and heirs, and he had a loan or a deposit in the hands of others, it is given to the weakest of them; and Rabbi Yoḥanan said about it: to the wife’s marriage contract, because of favor. Evidently one attends.
gershom:a1.1: Kulfei tavei: good blows I received from Avimi my teacher before I understood this teaching.
gershom:a2.1: And so he said to me: If he comes to proclaim consecutively, on every single day, he need proclaim only thirty; but if he proclaims only on Mondays and Thursdays, he must proclaim on the Mondays and Thursdays of sixty days.
gershom:a3.1: And even though when you count them there are only eighteen days: how so? When you begin counting sixty days from a Monday, they are eight weeks and four days. Eight weeks have sixteen days of proclamation, and those four days begin on a Monday and end on a Thursday: that makes eighteen.
gershom:a4.1: Since the matter extends: since these eighteen stretch over sixty days, people hear.
gershom:a5.1: One does not attend to the property of orphans while they are minors; but when they grow up, certainly one attends to selling it in order to pay.
gershom:a6.1: Unless interest is consuming it: their father had taken a loan at interest, and the orphans lose every day.
gershom:a7.1: Or for a wife’s marriage contract because of sustenance: to pay the marriage contract of their father’s wife, for as long as she has not collected her marriage contract she is sustained from the orphans, and they lose the sustenance.
gershom:a8.1: For they established for them: [the Sages gave] the orphans the earnings of their father’s wife, since she is sustained from theirs, and so they have no loss from the sustenance.
gershom:a9.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan says: for this reason one attends to the marriage contract, because sometimes her work does not match her sustenance, and the orphans lose.
gershom:a10.1: If we say: in order to pay a Persian creditor [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “Persian” where the Davidson English has “gentile”], will a Persian comply and wait until we proclaim for thirty [days]?
gershom:a11.1: And if he is consuming interest from the orphans, that is, that this is why one attends: do we let a Jewish creditor take interest?
gershom:a12.1: He establishes it with a wife’s marriage contract: and that is why one attends, since they lose sustenance.
gershom:a13.1: But according to Rav Asi: why does one attend to selling? There is no interest here!
gershom:a14.1: And according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, does it work out? Why proclaim? Let them give her marriage contract at once, and she will be removed from sustenance. Now we let her consume sustenance, which is certainly a loss until the days of proclamation end, and we take the proclamation, about which we do not know whether we gain for the orphans or not: it is uncertain whether they will add anything to the appraisal or not.
gershom:a15.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: This is not difficult. As for what you said, that we let her consume sustenance, which is a loss: we are dealing with one who claims her marriage contract in court, who has no sustenance.
gershom:a16.1: If so, that we are dealing with one who claims her marriage contract in court, we should not attend to her at all, neither to sell nor to proclaim, since she has already lost her sustenance.
gershom:a17.1: Since we attended to her at the outset, when she claims her marriage contract, we attend to her in the end and collect her marriage contract for her, and it needs a proclamation.
gershom:a18.1: In any case it is difficult for Rav Asi: who said one attends only for interest, and there is no interest here.
gershom:a19.1: Actually with a Persian creditor, who takes interest. And as for your difficulty, will a Persian wait for the proclamation: it is where he accepted upon himself to be judged, to wait for the proclamation, but he takes interest.
gershom:a20.1: Will a Persian comply and take inferior land? And if, like Rav Asi who said [one attends] because of interest, a Jew is consuming interest, do we let him, etc.
gershom:a21.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan it works out: since a wife’s marriage contract is from inferior land, and because she causes a loss through sustenance.
gershom:a22.1: Even from the husband himself she takes only inferior land; so what does it teach us with orphans?
gershom:a23.1: This is not difficult: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds like Rabbi Meir, that from the husband [it is] from intermediate land.
gershom:a24.1: That he accepted upon himself, under Jewish law, to take from orphans from inferior land, but he takes interest; therefore one attends. In order to give the wife her marriage contract and the creditor his debt: whether from the property of orphans or from consecrated property, for example where he consecrated his property and died, and this wife’s marriage contract and this creditor were upon him, and the orphans need to redeem the property from the Temple treasury in order to give the wife her marriage contract, etc.
gershom:a25.1: Whether according to this Sage or according to that Sage, as we answered: for a document that contains interest, both agree that one attends to a creditor because of interest. When the one obligated admits before his death that this wife’s marriage contract or this debt is still upon him, and instructed to give it.
gershom:a26.1: All of them too: those we answered above as speaking of a Persian creditor are really with a Jewish creditor. And why does one attend?
gershom:a27.1: When the one obligated admits, and instructed to give it.
gershom:a28.1: For a divorcée: whose husband divorced her and died.
gershom:a29.1: From the property of orphans: even though a divorcée has no sustenance.
gershom:a30.1: That of Rabbi Yoḥanan, “or for a wife’s marriage contract”: we teach it because of favor, so that women will know that they have a marriage contract from the orphans; even when they are divorced, one attends to them to collect their marriage contract, though they have no sustenance. And they will be agreeable to their husbands and not distress them, and through this they will find favor in their husbands’ eyes. Therefore we collect for a divorcée because of the favor of all women.
gershom:a31.1: Let them go after those who left them: that is, he would curse them that they not live long but go after their father, who left them by dying, since they consume what is not theirs.
gershom:a32.1: I would attend: in order to keep them from a prohibition.
gershom:a33.1: At the outset, what is the reason that he would not attend? Because Rav Pappa said: Repayment, etc.
gershom:a34.1: Say he placed bundles: the borrower placed [them with] the lender before his death, so that his debt would be repaid from them.
gershom:a35.1: The difference between them is when the one obligated admits at the time of his death that he still owes him. According to the one who says it is because of a mitzva, they do not pay, since orphans are not fit to perform a mitzva; according to the one who says it is because of bundles, since he admits, one cannot say he placed bundles.
gershom:a36.1: Or else: that they brought him to judgment and the court excommunicated the borrower to make him pay the lender, and he died in his excommunication. Here certainly one cannot say he placed bundles, and the orphans are obligated to pay; and according to the one who says it is because of a mitzva, they do not pay.
gershom:a37.1: They sent from there: where they excommunicated him and he died in his excommunication, we attend, for there certainly there is no need to worry that he placed bundles. But in general, even when the one obligated admits, we do not attend, since one can say that he admits he owes him, but there is a concern that he placed bundles [as a pledge].
gershom:a38.1: And the halakha follows Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, who said we are concerned about bundles.
gershom:b1.1: Granted, according to Rav Huna, he establishes it where the one obligated admits: that is why we attend, since he did not place bundles.
gershom:b2.1: But according to Rav Pappa, who said orphans are not fit to perform a mitzva, why do we attend?
gershom:b3.1: And if you wish, say with a Persian creditor: and because of interest; and he accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law regarding the proclamation.
gershom:b4.1: Rava said, because of a receipt: Rav Naḥman did not attend at first, because one can say that perhaps the borrower had a receipt showing that the lender’s document was paid, and it was lost; therefore one does not attend.
gershom:b5.1: They taught only: that she is believed with an oath and we are not concerned about a receipt, only for a wife’s marriage contract, because of favor.
gershom:b6.1: And if you are concerned about a receipt, there too let us be concerned: why does a creditor collect in his absence with an oath? Let us be concerned that perhaps the borrower has a receipt.
gershom:b7.1: He said to him: There, with a creditor who collects in his absence, we say we are not concerned about a receipt, for the reason we stated; but in general we are concerned about a receipt.
gershom:b8.1: And if the orphans’ father said before his death, “Give to so-and-so,” the court attends and gives.
gershom:b9.1: And if he said, “Give this field and this hundred to so-and-so,” one attends and does not install a steward for the orphans in this matter to litigate with the lender; since he said explicitly “this field and this hundred,” they give it to him.
gershom:b10.1: But if he said “a field” unspecified or “a hundred” unspecified, one attends and installs a steward for the orphans, who will argue that perhaps he did not mean this field but that one, and push him off to inferior land.
gershom:b11.1: But if it is found that he had a field that is not his, and he said “Give it to him”: that it was not the dead man’s but this man’s, to whom he instructed it be given. Certainly they give him that field, which was not his, even though he said “a field” unspecified, and they do not install a steward. Since there are witnesses who say that it was not his but this man’s, no steward is needed, for we do not presume that witnesses who say it is this man’s are liars.
gershom:b12.1: In all of them one installs a steward: even where he says “this field and this hundred.”
rashi:b1.1: If we say with a gentile creditor: who does not want to wait until they grow up, will he comply and wait the days of proclamation?
rashi:b5.1: Come and hear: what was taught above about the proclamation: “in order to give to a wife,” etc.
rashi:b5.2: Will he comply: with the days of proclamation?
rashi:b8.1: Rava said: [the reason] that one does not attend to the property of orphans.
rashi:b8.2: Because of a receipt: perhaps their father had a receipt on this document, showing that he paid it, and the orphans do not know where it is.
rashi:b8.3: One who collects in his absence: for example, where the husband sent her a bill of divorce from overseas.
rashi:b9.1: They taught only: that the court goes down to a person’s property in his absence only for a wife’s marriage contract, because of favor; but a creditor must wait until he returns.
rashi:b11.1: And if he said: [if] their father [said] “Give,” one attends.
rashi:b11.2: This field and this hundred: if he said “Give this field to so-and-so for his debt,” or “this hundred,” one attends to give it to him, and there is no need to install a steward for the orphans over it.
rashi:b11.3: A field unspecified and a hundred unspecified, one attends and installs a steward: for the orphans, to choose a good portion for them and collect for this man from the inferior land.
rashi:b12.1: But if a field is found in the orphans’ hands that was not their father’s but stolen, one attends to remove the stolen property from them, and no steward is needed.
rashi:b12.2: In all of them: even “this field” and “this hundred,” one attends and installs a steward, except for a field found not to be his, where no steward is needed, but it is removed from them at once; for we do not presume that the witnesses who testify about the robbery are liars.
tosafot:b8.1: Rava said: Because of a receipt. The difference between Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, who said because of bundles, and Rava, who said because of a receipt, is where [the father] handed his documents to one person before witnesses and said that he had no documents other than those he had handed him. Now there is no concern about a receipt, since he handed all his documents to this man, and had he had a receipt he would have handed it to him; but about bundles there is still a concern.
tosafot:b8.2: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said to Rava: But are we concerned about a receipt? Didn’t we learn: One who collects in his absence…; and if we are concerned about a receipt, here too let us be concerned. And if you will say: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, should find it difficult for himself too: let us be concerned about bundles! One can say: it was plain to Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, that because of bundles one should not refuse to collect in his absence, so that not everyone will take his fellow’s money and settle overseas; but because of the concern about a receipt, it did not occur to him to say so. That is why he asked him, “Let us be concerned about a receipt,” and he answered him: There it is as we say, so that not everyone, etc.
tosafot:b11.1: And if he said “Give,” one attends: Seemingly this means “give the debt,” and this is like Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, that where the one obligated admits, one attends. And this needs study: why did it leave the wording “the one obligated admits”? Perhaps it uses this wording “give” because it fits both a debt and a gift: if their father instructed the orphans to give a gift, they give it, if he instructed it as one who distributes his property as a gift, all of it or part of it, and made an act of acquisition. And it somewhat appears so too, that it speaks of a gift, since it says: “this field” and “this hundred,” one attends to him.
tosafot:b11.2: And if he said “Give,” one attends: And it is puzzling: it is obvious that if he said “give,” one attends, since he gave it as a gift! And the Ri says: “one attends” was needed. It uses the wording “give” because it ends with “this field and this hundred,” to which “give” applies. Furthermore, there is an admission, which does not suffice unless he said “give” about them, or “you are my witnesses,” for example where he admitted on his own. (And what we say) in the chapter Get Pashut (Bava Batra 174b): A dangerously ill person who said, “Give a hundred to so-and-so”: if he said “give,” they give; if he did not say “give,” they do not give, since a person is apt [to say such things] so that his sons will not appear wealthy. But if they claimed from him and he admitted, even without “you are my witnesses” and without saying “give,” they give, since a person does not jest at the time of death, as is evident at the end of the chapter Get Pashut (Bava Batra 175b).
tosafot:b11.3: And one does not install a steward: since he said “this field and this hundred,” there is no need to install a steward to find out whether he paid or not and has a receipt. [Otherwise] one installs the steward to find out whether he paid or not and has a receipt: they install the steward to look for the receipt among the dead man’s belongings, or to find some testimony that he placed bundles. And if you will say: since he said “give,” even if he owes nothing they should give it to him, since it is an instruction on account of death, and it would be a mere gift! One can say: he thinks he is obligated because of his debt, and not as any gift; therefore it is to be given only to one to whom he is obligated. And so it is evident in the chapter Get Pashut (Bava Batra 174b), about the case I cited above: [if] he said “give,” he has validated his document. Evidently, because he acknowledges him when he says “give,” it is as though the document were validated; but had he not been obligated, he would not give it as a gift.
tosafot:b12.1: The Nehardeans say: In all of them one attends and installs a steward. That is, in all of them: “this field” and “this hundred.”
tosafot:b13.1: In brief: Rav Ashi means that in general, where there is a concern about bundles, as in Rav Asi’s statement, one does not attend to the property of orphans; and where one does attend, as with “this field and this hundred,” where Rava said one attends without a steward, we do not hold like Rava but install a steward, as the Nehardeans say, except for a field found not to be his, where no steward is needed since we do not presume that witnesses are liars. Question: in HaGozel Batra (Bava Kamma 112a), Rabbi Yirmeya’s brother-in-law shut the door in his face; Rabbi Abba said he was claiming what was his own, and when [Rabbi Yirmeya] said he would bring witnesses that he had held it in the father’s lifetime, Rabbi Abba said: Does one accept testimony not in the presence of the litigant? How is that different from our passage, where a field found not to be his is taken and the testimony accepted even though the orphans are minors? Answer: there it had originally been the orphan’s father’s, so even with witnesses that [Rabbi Yirmeya] held it, the testimony should not be accepted; and that is not presuming the witnesses are liars, since the father may have had some arrangement with him to hold it although it was the father’s. Here the witnesses testify that he stole it, so it was certainly stolen; we do not say that perhaps he later bought it, since it came to him by robbery, and so the testimony may be accepted in the litigant’s absence. So too in HaGozel Batra (Bava Kamma 112b), Rabbi Yehoshua says that a child who seized his father’s slaves, or went down into another’s field and said “It is mine,” is not told to wait until he grows up, and the Talmud concludes that it is taken from him because the father’s possession was never established: there are matters where testimony is accepted in the litigant’s absence. Therefore it seems that where the one obligated admitted an oral loan, one attends: witnesses testify before the court that they heard the father’s admission, and the debt is collected from the orphans on their testimony, since the admission is clear, like a field found not to be his. Still, with liability arising from the orphans themselves, even when we know clearly that no bundles were placed, one does not attend, as in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ Arba’a VaḤamisha (Bava Kamma 39a), where an orphans’ ox that did damage is exempt because one does not attend; the Ri explained that bundles do not apply there, yet one does not attend because testimony is not accepted in the litigant’s absence.
